parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 9. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man interviewing a woman for a survey about local parks. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5. Interviewer: Excuse me, have you got a few minutes to answer some questions? We're doing a survey for the city council about local parks. Kate: Sure, I've got a bit of time. Interviewer: Thanks very much. Can I start with your name? Kate: Yes, it's Kate Dunmore. Interviewer: Could you spell your surname for me? Kate: D, U, N, M, O, R, E. Interviewer: Thanks. And which year were you born? Kate: Nineteen eighty-seven. Interviewer: And do you live locally? Kate: Yes, in Fairfield, just north of the river. Interviewer: And how often would you say you visit parks in the city? Kate: Oh, several times a week, especially in the summer. Riverside Park is the nearest to us, so that's the one we use most, but we sometimes go to Castle Park at the weekend, because it's bigger. Interviewer: OK, thanks. I'll just put that down. Interviewer: Great. Now I'd like to ask you about your most recent visit to Riverside Park. When was that? Kate: Today, actually. It's the eleventh, isn't it? Interviewer: No, it's the 12th of June today. Kate: Oh, yes, of course. Well, today then. Interviewer: And what was the main reason for your visit? Kate: I was taking my son to the playground. We go about twice a week. I did a bit of jogging round the lake while he was playing, but the main reason was really the playground. Interviewer: And how did you get to the park? Kate: I cycled, with my son on the back. I used to take the bus, but it's so unreliable. It hardly ever comes on time, so I gave up on it. Interviewer: I see. And which entrance did you use? Kate: The Ashby Gate, on the east side. Interviewer: Is that A, S, H, B, Y? Kate: That's right. Interviewer: And roughly how long did you spend in the park today? Kate: About an hour and a half. My son would stay all day if I let him! Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. Interviewer: Have you noticed any problems in the park? Kate: Well, the toilets near the playground were closed again today, which is really annoying when you've got a small child. They're usually quite clean, so that's not the problem. But there's been a sign saying they're being repaired for weeks now. Interviewer: I'll make a note of that. Anything else? Kate: Yes, there aren't enough bins. People leave rubbish on the grass because the bins are always full. There are plenty of benches, though. That's one thing the park does well. Interviewer: Do you use the park for anything else? Kate: On Sundays, I often go to the market by the lake. They sell lovely fresh bread and vegetables. I don't go to the cafe much, because it's quite expensive. Interviewer: And is there anything you'd like to see improved? Kate: In the summer, there's hardly any shade in the playground, and the children get really hot. More trees would be nice, or even just some canvas covers over the play equipment. Interviewer: That's a good suggestion. And do you visit the park in the winter? Kate: Not really. It gets dark so early, and there's very little lighting along the paths, so I don't feel safe walking through the park after about four o'clock. Interviewer: That's very useful. Thank you so much for your time. Interviewer: Oh, one last thing. Would you be happy for us to contact you about future consultations on the park? Kate: Yes, that's fine. I'm usually quite happy to give my opinion! Kate: No problem. I hope something changes! That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a woman talking to a group of people who are interested in becoming volunteers for a dog rescue charity. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Speaker: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming along to find out more about volunteering with Second Chance Dogs. We rescue around four hundred dogs every year, and we simply couldn't do it without our volunteers. Before I start, I must apologise about the temperature in here. The heating in this part of the building broke down this morning, and the engineer can't come until tomorrow, so please do keep your coats on. At least there are enough chairs for everyone this time, and we'll only be here for about forty minutes. Then there's tea in the next room, which is much warmer, I promise. Speaker: One question we're often asked is whether you need experience with dogs. Well, it certainly helps, but it isn't essential. Some of our most wonderful volunteers had never owned a dog before they joined us. What matters much more is that you're patient and reliable. Dogs that have been neglected need people they can trust, people who turn up when they say they will. We also get asked about age. Volunteers need to be at least eighteen to foster a dog, but younger people can help at the centre with an adult. Speaker: Another common question is about training. Everyone starts with an introductory session, but training doesn't stop there. It carries on the whole time you're with us, with regular sessions throughout the year as you take on new tasks. Most of it is run by our experienced volunteers rather than by our vets, who are usually far too busy. And it all takes place in person, here at the centre, not online. Speaker: Now, before you apply, there are a couple of things I'd ask you to think about carefully. We don't need to know why you want to volunteer. People have all sorts of reasons, and they're all fine with us. Your income isn't an issue either, because we cover the cost of food and vet bills for any dog you look after. And you don't need a big garden, by the way. Plenty of our foster carers live in flats. But please think about whether you have any other animals at home. Some of our dogs are very nervous around cats, for example, so we need to know. And think honestly about how much time you actually spend at home. A dog that's left alone all day won't settle, however loving the family is. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Speaker: Right, let's look at some of the roles we need volunteers for, and what would help you in each one. First, fundraising. You don't need any sales experience for this. We're always grateful for help with collection tins, but what we really need are people who can come up with fresh, original ideas for raising money, because the same old events can start to feel a bit stale. Speaker: Then there's dog walking. Many of our dogs need several long walks every day, often on steep, hilly paths around the centre, so you'll need to be reasonably fit. Speaker: We also need volunteers to carry out home visits. Before a dog goes to a new family, someone visits the home to check that it's suitable. You'll be given a long checklist to go through, but you won't be able to write much down during the visit, as that can make families nervous. So a good memory is really useful for this role. Speaker: Our social media team shares the stories of dogs that are looking for new homes. The better the photos, the faster a dog finds a family, so if you're good with a camera, this could be the role for you. Last year, one of our volunteers took a photograph of an elderly greyhound that was shared thousands of times, and he found a home within two days. Speaker: And finally, we run classes for people who've just adopted puppies. You don't need to be a qualified trainer, but it helps if you know something about nutrition, because new owners always have lots of questions about what, and how much, to feed their puppies. Right, does anyone have any questions? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two journalism students, Isla and Kai, discussing a talk by a newspaper editor that they have just attended. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26. Kai: Hi, Isla. What did you think of the talk? Isla: Hi, Kai. It was great, once I could actually hear her. Kai: Why, were you stuck behind someone? Isla: No, I had a good seat, and for once I wasn't late. But the microphone wasn't working properly for the first ten minutes, and from the back of the hall I could hardly hear a word she said. Kai: Oh, I was near the front, so I didn't notice. Anyway, what did you think of it? Isla: It was really interesting, especially what she said about jobs. Kai: Yes. We all know newspapers are struggling, so I expected her to tell us it would be hard to find work. Isla: Me too. But I had no idea there were so many different kinds of roles now. Data journalism, podcasts, fact-checking, video production. Kai: Neither did I. That was a real eye-opener. Isla: I'd never even heard of some of them. I'm going to look into data journalism, actually. It sounds really interesting. Kai: Me too. Although I think I might be better at video. Isla: She was quite tough on us, though, wasn't she? Every time someone asked a question, she'd say, that's what students always think, and then explain why we were wrong. Kai: Yes, it felt a bit unfair at times. We're only in our first year, after all. We can't be expected to know everything already. Isla: Exactly. Do you think school prepared us well for this? Kai: Well, we had loads of careers talks, which was good, and they came at the right time, just before we chose our university courses. But they were always given by teachers, and none of them had ever worked in the media. Isla: I agree. It would have been much better to hear from people like today's speaker, who really know the industry. Kai: So, has the talk made you think about which area of journalism you want to go into? Isla: Not really. I want to try everything during the course and then decide at the end. Kai: I think it's better to choose a specialism now and start building a portfolio straight away. Isla: Well, we'll have to agree to disagree on that. Kai: She also said we should expect to work unpaid for a while, doing internships. I'm prepared for that. It's just how the industry works at the moment. Isla: I'm not so sure. I don't think anyone should have to work for nothing. Kai: Well, I hope you're right. But I'd rather be realistic about it. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30. Isla: I loved hearing about her first job on a local paper. Kai: Me too. She was very honest about the mistakes she made. Isla: Like that story about the local council, where she only spoke to one person and didn't check what he'd told her with anyone else. Kai: And it turned out to be completely wrong. She said she'd never rely on a single source again. Isla: And she missed the deadline for her first front-page story because she kept rewriting the opening paragraph. Her editor had to fill the space with something else. Kai: She didn't argue with her editor about it, though. She said she was far too scared! Isla: And she wasn't expecting to become famous, or to earn a lot of money. She said all she wanted back then was experience. Kai: She also said that working on a local paper teaches you things you'd never learn at a big national one. Isla: Like what readers actually complain about. She said the letters page told her more about her readers than any survey could. Kai: Yes, that would be really useful to know. And the website shows exactly which stories people read and which ones they ignore. Isla: Definitely. That's the kind of information every journalist needs. I'm less convinced by her point that you learn to write more quickly, though. We'll get plenty of practice at that on the course. Kai: True. And I don't think knowing how the printing process works matters much these days. She also mentioned the advertising side of things, but I can't say either of us is interested in that. Isla: No, not at all! That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a zoology student giving a presentation about efforts to save vultures in India. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation today, I want to talk about efforts to save vultures in India. Thirty years ago, vultures were one of the most common large birds in the country, and it's been estimated that there were tens of millions of them. Then, during the nineteen nineties, their numbers began to fall, and within about fifteen years, the populations of three species had dropped by more than ninety-five per cent. I first became interested in this topic after reading about the Parsi community in Mumbai, who traditionally placed their dead on high towers so that vultures could remove the bodies. When the vultures disappeared, this ancient practice suddenly became very difficult. Student: For a while, nobody knew why. Some scientists suspected a disease, others blamed a lack of food. Eventually, researchers discovered the cause: a painkiller that farmers were giving to sick cattle. Vultures feed on the bodies of dead animals, and when they ate the carcasses of cattle that had recently been treated with the drug, even a tiny amount was enough to cause fatal kidney failure. Student: The loss of the vultures created serious problems. Vultures are extremely efficient at clearing away dead animals. A group of them can strip a carcass in less than an hour. Without them, carcasses were left lying around to rot, and the numbers of wild dogs increased dramatically because of all the extra food. That was a real danger to people, because dogs spread rabies, and studies suggest that the rise in dog numbers led to thousands of additional human deaths from the disease. Farmers also lost a free and efficient service that had disposed of dead livestock for centuries. Student: In 2006, the government banned the use of the drug on animals, and conservationists set up breeding centres to build up the number of vultures. The birds are kept in large aviaries, where they can fly and nest in conditions as close as possible to the wild. To speed up breeding, staff sometimes remove the first eggs a female lays and hatch them in incubators. This encourages the female to lay again, so each pair can produce more chicks in a season. Student: Releasing captive-bred vultures into the wild has to be done very carefully. Before they're released, the birds spend several months in a special aviary at the release site, so that they can get used to the local climate and see the wild vultures that visit the area. Each bird is fitted with coloured tags on its wings, so that observers can identify it from a distance, and many also carry a small transmitter so that their movements can be tracked. The first releases took place only after several years of careful preparation, including surveys to make sure that the harmful drug was no longer being used in the surrounding area. Student: Of course, released birds need a safe supply of food. So conservationists have set up feeding sites, known as vulture restaurants, where the carcasses of animals that haven't been treated with harmful drugs are provided. These also make it easier to count and monitor the birds. Student: So, has it worked? It's still early days, but the results are encouraging. Released birds have survived and joined wild flocks, and there are signs that some of them have begun to breed in the wild. The project has also involved local communities. Schools visit the breeding centres, and children take part in counting birds, which has helped to raise awareness of how important vultures are. Many young people who once saw vultures as frightening or dirty now see them as valuable neighbours. Student: There's still a long way to go, and other harmful drugs remain a threat, but the vulture programme shows what can be achieved when scientists, governments and local people work together. Are there any questions? That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

Dogs that have been neglected need people they can trust, people who turn up when they say they will. We also get asked about age. Volunteers need to be at least eighteen to foster a dog, but younger people can help at the centre with an adult. Speaker: Another common question is about training. Everyone starts with an introductory session, but training doesn't stop there. It carries on the whole time you're with us, with regular sessions throughout the year as you take on new tasks. Most of it is run by our experienced volunteers rather than by our vets, who are usually far too busy. And it all takes place in person, here at the centre, not online. Speaker: Now, before you apply, there are a couple of things I'd ask you to think about carefully. We don't need to know why you want to volunteer. People have all sorts of reasons, and they're all fine with us. Your income isn't an issue either, because we cover the cost of food and vet bills for any dog you look after. And you don't need a big garden, by the way. Plenty of our foster carers live in flats. But please think about whether you have any other animals at home. Some of our dogs are very nervous around cats, for example, so we need to know. And think honestly about how much time you actually spend at home. A dog that's left alone all day won't settle, however loving the family is. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Speaker: Right, let's look at some of the roles we need volunteers for, and what would help you in each one. First, fundraising. You don't need any sales experience for this. We're always grateful for help with collection tins, but what we really need are people who can come up with fresh, original ideas for raising money, because the same old events can start to feel a bit stale. Speaker: Then there's dog walking. Many of our dogs need several long walks every day, often on steep, hilly paths around the centre, so you'll need to be reasonably fit. Speaker: We also need volunteers to carry out home visits. Before a dog goes to a new family, someone visits the home to check that it's suitable. You'll be given a long checklist to go through, but you won't be able to write much down during the visit, as that can make families nervous. So a good memory is really useful for this role. Speaker: Our social media team shares the stories of dogs that are looking for new homes. The better the photos, the faster a dog finds a family, so if you're good with a camera, this could be the role for you. Last year, one of our volunteers took a photograph of an elderly greyhound that was shared thousands of times, and he found a home within two days. Speaker: And finally, we run classes for people who've just adopted puppies. You don't need to be a qualified trainer, but it helps if you know something about nutrition, because new owners always have lots of questions about what, and how much, to feed their puppies. Right, does anyone have any questions? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two journalism students, Isla and Kai, discussing a talk by a newspaper editor that they have just attended. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26. Kai: Hi, Isla. What did you think of the talk? Isla: Hi, Kai. It was great, once I could actually hear her. Kai: Why, were you stuck behind someone? Isla: No, I had a good seat, and for once I wasn't late. But the microphone wasn't working properly for the first ten minutes, and from the back of the hall I could hardly hear a word she said. Kai: Oh, I was near the front, so I didn't notice. Anyway, what did you think of it? Isla: It was really interesting, especially what she said about jobs. Kai: Yes. We all know newspapers are struggling, so I expected her to tell us it would be hard to find work. Isla: Me too. But I had no idea there were so many different kinds of roles now. Data journalism, podcasts, fact-checking, video production. Kai: Neither did I. That was a real eye-opener. Isla: I'd never even heard of some of them. I'm going to look into data journalism, actually. It sounds really interesting. Kai: Me too. Although I think I might be better at video. Isla: She was quite tough on us, though, wasn't she? Every time someone asked a question, she'd say, that's what students always think, and then explain why we were wrong. Kai: Yes, it felt a bit unfair at times. We're only in our first year, after all. We can't be expected to know everything already. Isla: Exactly. Do you think school prepared us well for this? Kai: Well, we had loads of careers talks, which was good, and they came at the right time, just before we chose our university courses. But they were always given by teachers, and none of them had ever worked in the media. Isla: I agree. It would have been much better to hear from people like today's speaker, who really know the industry. Kai: So, has the talk made you think about which area of journalism you want to go into? Isla: Not really. I want to try everything during the course and then decide at the end. Kai: I think it's better to choose a specialism now and start building a portfolio straight away. Isla: Well, we'll have to agree to disagree on that. Kai: She also said we should expect to work unpaid for a while, doing internships. I'm prepared for that. It's just how the industry works at the moment. Isla: I'm not so sure. I don't think anyone should have to work for nothing. Kai: Well, I hope you're right. But I'd rather be realistic about it. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30. Isla: I loved hearing about her first job on a local paper. Kai: Me too. She was very honest about the mistakes she made. Isla: Like that story about the local council, where she only spoke to one person and didn't check what he'd told her with anyone else. Kai: And it turned out to be completely wrong. She said she'd never rely on a single source again. Isla: And she missed the deadline for her first front-page story because she kept rewriting the opening paragraph. Her editor had to fill the space with something else. Kai: She didn't argue with her editor about it, though. She said she was far too scared! Isla: And she wasn't expecting to become famous, or to earn a lot of money. She said all she wanted back then was experience. Kai: She also said that working on a local paper teaches you things you'd never learn at a big national one. Isla: Like what readers actually complain about. She said the letters page told her more about her readers than any survey could. Kai: Yes, that would be really useful to know. And the website shows exactly which stories people read and which ones they ignore. Isla: Definitely. That's the kind of information every journalist needs. I'm less convinced by her point that you learn to write more quickly, though. We'll get plenty of practice at that on the course. Kai: True. And I don't think knowing how the printing process works matters much these days. She also mentioned the advertising side of things, but I can't say either of us is interested in that. Isla: No, not at all! That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a zoology student giving a presentation about efforts to save vultures in India. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation today, I want to talk about efforts to save vultures in India. Thirty years ago, vultures were one of the most common large birds in the country, and it's been estimated that there were tens of millions of them. Then, during the nineteen nineties, their numbers began to fall, and within about fifteen years, the populations of three species had dropped by more than ninety-five per cent. I first became interested in this topic after reading about the Parsi community in Mumbai, who traditionally placed their dead on high towers so that vultures could remove the bodies. When the vultures disappeared, this ancient practice suddenly became very difficult. Student: For a while, nobody knew why. Some scientists suspected a disease, others blamed a lack of food. Eventually, researchers discovered the cause: a painkiller that farmers were giving to sick cattle. Vultures feed on the bodies of dead animals, and when they ate the carcasses of cattle that had recently been treated with the drug, even a tiny amount was enough to cause fatal kidney failure. Student: The loss of the vultures created serious problems. Vultures are extremely efficient at clearing away dead animals. A group of them can strip a carcass in less than an hour. Without them, carcasses were left lying around to rot, and the numbers of wild dogs increased dramatically because of all the extra food. That was a real danger to people, because dogs spread rabies, and studies suggest that the rise in dog numbers led to thousands of additional human deaths from the disease. Farmers also lost a free and efficient service that had disposed of dead livestock for centuries. Student: In 2006, the government banned the use of the drug on animals, and conservationists set up breeding centres to build up the number of vultures. The birds are kept in large aviaries, where they can fly and nest in conditions as close as possible to the wild. To speed up breeding, staff sometimes remove the first eggs a female lays and hatch them in incubators. This encourages the female to lay again, so each pair can produce more chicks in a season. Student: Releasing captive-bred vultures into the wild has to be done very carefully. Before they're released, the birds spend several months in a special aviary at the release site, so that they can get used to the local climate and see the wild vultures that visit the area. Each bird is fitted with coloured tags on its wings, so that observers can identify it from a distance, and many also carry a small transmitter so that their movements can be tracked. The first releases took place only after several years of careful preparation, including surveys to make sure that the harmful drug was no longer being used in the surrounding area. Student: Of course, released birds need a safe supply of food. So conservationists have set up feeding sites, known as vulture restaurants, where the carcasses of animals that haven't been treated with harmful drugs are provided. These also make it easier to count and monitor the birds. Student: So, has it worked? It's still early days, but the results are encouraging. Released birds have survived and joined wild flocks, and there are signs that some of them have begun to breed in the wild. The project has also involved local communities. Schools visit the breeding centres, and children take part in counting birds, which has helped to raise awareness of how important vultures are. Many young people who once saw vultures as frightening or dirty now see them as valuable neighbours. Student: There's still a long way to go, and other harmful drugs remain a threat, but the vulture programme shows what can be achieved when scientists, governments and local people work together. Are there any questions? That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
